title: Gold Drops Below $4,000 as Iran Conflict Fuels Fed Rate Hike Fears
excerpt: The precious metal posts its worst weekly loss in six weeks as rising oil prices from U.S.-Iran hostilities revive inflation concerns and push rate-hike odds to 73% before December.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gold fell to $3,975, its lowest in eight months, before recovering slightly.
  • Crude oil prices surged over 10% amid U.S.-Iran tensions, raising inflation concerns.
  • Traders estimate 73% odds of a Fed rate hike before December, with 55% for September.
  • In India, gold prices fell to ₹1.42 lakh per 10 grams, with discounts up to $19 per ounce.

  • Spot gold fell to $3,975 on Friday — an eight-month low — before recovering to $3,983, down more than 3% for the week ending July 17.
  • Crude oil surged over 10% this week as U.S.-Iran hostilities intensified around the Strait of Hormuz, reviving inflation fears that override gold's traditional safe-haven appeal.
  • Traders now price in roughly 73% odds of a Fed rate hike before December and 55% odds of a September move, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
  • In India, gold traded at discounts of up to $19 per ounce as price volatility crushed retail demand, with 24-karat prices falling to around ₹1.42 lakh per 10 grams.

War Drives Oil Up — and Gold Down

Gold ended the week of July 13–17 near $3,984 an ounce, logging its steepest five-day decline in six weeks despite — or more accurately, because of — an escalating shooting war in the Persian Gulf.

The U.S. Central Command completed a sixth consecutive night of strikes against Iran, hitting bridges in Hormozgan province, the Chabahar maritime control tower, and a railway terminal near Bandar Abbas. Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on U.S.-allied bases in Kuwait and Jordan. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Tehran had asked Yemen's Houthi movement to stand ready to close the Red Sea oil route if Washington targets Iranian power infrastructure.

The escalation sent Brent crude above $85 a barrel and WTI past $79, both up more than 11% on the week. In a conventional market, that kind of geopolitical risk would have driven buyers into gold. Instead, the metal fell through the psychologically important $4,000 level.

The Counterintuitive Mechanism

The explanation is mechanistically straightforward: in 2026, gold has stopped trading as a safe haven and started trading as a pure real-rate instrument. Higher crude raises transport and production costs, feeds into headline inflation, keeps the Federal Reserve hawkish, lifts real yields, and raises the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays nothing.

"The recent price action suggests that markets are placing greater weight on the prospect of higher-for-longer U.S. interest rates than on gold's traditional safe-haven demand."

- Soojin Kim, MUFG

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan reinforced that stance this week, saying that positive news on consumer and wholesale prices "still wasn't good enough" and calling for modestly higher rates. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said he would be open to raising rates if inflation does not show near-term improvement.

According to the CME FedWatch Tool, traders now price in nearly 55% odds of a rate hike in September and roughly 73% odds of at least one increase before December. The Dollar Index climbed to 100.79, adding further pressure on dollar-denominated gold.

Softer CPI Offered Only Temporary Relief

Tuesday's June CPI print had briefly lifted bullion. The energy index fell 5.7% in June — its sharpest monthly drop since April 2020 — driven by gasoline declining 9.7%. Core CPI came in flat at 0.0% month-over-month, and the Producer Price Index released Wednesday confirmed the downward trend.

But the disinflation narrative lasted barely 48 hours. Thursday's oil spike, powered by the intensifying military strikes, reminded markets that June's soft inflation data was built on a crude price trough near $70 on July 1 that has since reversed sharply. The July CPI print, due August 12, will carry the impact of $80-plus crude through the energy component.

India Demand Freezes as Volatility Bites

For Indian consumers and the diaspora, the gold selloff has created a paradox: lower international prices but deepening uncertainty. Domestic 24-karat gold was trading near ₹1.42 lakh per 10 grams as of mid-July, down from a record ₹1.76 lakh hit on January 29 — a decline of nearly 20%.

Dealers in India quoted discounts of up to $19 per ounce over official domestic prices, widening sharply from premiums of up to $5 just a week earlier, according to Reuters. "Retail buying has slowed, and most transactions are now exchanges of old jewellery for new," a Mumbai-based bullion dealer told the news agency. Ashok Jain of Mumbai wholesaler Chenaji Narsinghji said buyers were "waiting for a bigger drop" before committing.

Meanwhile, RBI data showed India's gold reserves rose by $24 million to $105.23 billion in the week ended July 10. India's broader forex reserves climbed by $964 million to $675.16 billion, with gold accounting for roughly 15.6% of the total — a share that has been rising steadily amid the central bank's diversification push.

What Comes Next

Gold is technically trapped. The 2026 low of $3,941 sits just 1% below spot, while the first meaningful resistance at $4,002 is less than half a percent above. Every major moving average — the 20-day at $4,081, the 200-day near $4,496 — sits overhead.

"Upside in gold requires oil prices to ease off further and hawkish rhetoric to dial down."

- Christopher Wong, OCBC

UBS's Chief Investment Office has maintained a 12-month target of $5,200, citing robust central bank buying as a structural floor. Central banks purchased a net 244 tonnes of gold in Q1 2026 alone. But the near-term path depends almost entirely on one variable: whether the Fed hikes.

For Indian households — the world's second-largest gold consumers — the coming weeks present a high-stakes calculation. Wedding and festival season inventories typically build from August onward. If prices hold near ₹1.42 lakh, dealers expect a wave of restocking. If the war pushes oil higher and triggers a Fed hike, gold could test the $3,941 floor and take domestic prices closer to ₹1.38 lakh, levels not seen since early March.
